children.title: VIPR Certificate Family
children.top_down_role: General proof logs for mixed-integer linear optimization results.

knowledge_statements.title: VIPR Certificate Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract mathematical contract for VIPR-style mixed-integer optimization proof logs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational mixed-integer linear instance \(I\) and claimed result \(R\), a VIPR-family certificate is a finite sequence \(C=(s_1,\ldots,s_t)\) whose steps cite input constraints or earlier steps and declare an admitted inference rule with exact rational data. A conforming checker accepts only when every cited object exists, every rule side condition holds, all local scopes are respected, and the terminal steps certify \(R\), such as infeasibility, a global objective bound, or optimality together with a feasible solution. The mathematical guarantee is conditional: acceptance establishes \(R\) only for the precise rule set and file semantics implemented by the verified certificate specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A VIPR-style certificate is a finite exact proof log whose checked terminal derivation supports an MILP result under the format’s specified inference rules.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) has exact rational constraint data.
Every step uses a rule admitted by the governing VIPR specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Check}(I,C,R)=\mathrm{accept}\Longrightarrow R\text{ holds for }I\), provided the checker and rule specification are sound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record cannot reliably characterize the VIPR certificate family without identifying a particular VIPR specification, version, admitted rules, terminal claims, and format semantics.

children.title: Independent Certificate Checkers
children.top_down_role: Verification systems separated from the producing solver.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Certificate Checkers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness contract for verification separated from the producing optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a solver producing a claim \(R\) and certificate \(C\) for instance \(I\), and let \(V\) be a checker implemented independently of \(S\). The checker must parse \(I\) and \(C\) without trusting solver-internal state and accept only after verifying every referenced datum and inference rule. If \(V\) is sound, then \(V(I,C,R)=\mathrm{accept}\) implies that \(R\) holds for \(I\), irrespective of how \(S\) generated \(C\). Independence reduces shared implementation faults but does not itself prove checker soundness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent checker trusts only the instance and certificate; its acceptance implies the result only when its parser, arithmetic, and inference rules are sound.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) does not rely on unrecorded state from \(S\).
Every acceptance path of \(V\) implements sound inference rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(I,C,R)=\mathrm{accept}\Longrightarrow R\text{ holds for }I\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: verifier soundness gives the displayed acceptance implication

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Principle is an appropriate kind for this leaf, and the conditional soundness statement is plausible, but an independent-checker architecture or verification source is required.

children.title: Exact Rational Checking
children.top_down_role: Certificate validation entirely in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Rational Checking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic certificate validation over canonical rational arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an instance and certificate whose numerical fields denote rationals. Parse each value as a reduced pair \((p,q)\in\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z_{>0}\). Process certificate steps in dependency order, evaluating sums, products, comparisons, floors, and linear identities in \(\mathbb Q\), using integer cross-multiplication for comparisons and rejecting malformed denominators, missing references, failed side conditions, or unequal identities. Accept and output the certified claim only if every step and terminal condition succeeds; otherwise reject. Because no tolerance is used, acceptance concerns the exact rational instance represented by the input, not a nearby floating-point instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parse all numbers as rationals, check every derivation with integer arithmetic and no tolerances, and accept only when all steps and terminal conditions hold exactly.
assumptions_latex: Every numeric token has an unambiguous rational interpretation.
Integer arithmetic is exact and resource exhaustion is reported as non-acceptance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns \(\mathrm{accept}\) only when every prescribed rational equality, inequality, and rule condition is exact.

notation.meaning: canonical numerator-denominator representation of a rational

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical fractions and integer cross-multiplication implement exact rational predicates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the appropriate kind and the arithmetic procedure is plausible, but no certificate-checker reference supports the parsing, rejection, dependency-order, and resource-exhaustion semantics.

children.title: Safe Rational Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of checkable objects from floating-point computations.

children.title: Rational Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of rational certificate objects from numerical output.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded reconstruction of a rational number from a modular residue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given integers \(m>1\), \(0\le r<m\), and bounds \(A,B\ge1\) satisfying \(2AB<m\), seek coprime integers \(a,b\) with \(|a|\le A\), \(0<b\le B\), and \(a\equiv rb\pmod m\). Apply the extended Euclidean algorithm, equivalently continued-fraction convergents of \(r/m\), to enumerate the bounded candidate determined by these inequalities. Return \(a/b\) only after checking the bounds, congruence, and \(\gcd(a,b)=1\); otherwise report failure. Under \(2AB<m\), at most one reduced rational satisfies all conditions, so successful validated reconstruction is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended Euclidean reconstruction recovers the unique bounded reduced fraction matching a residue modulo m when the numerator and denominator bounds satisfy twice their product below m.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B\ge1\) and \(2AB<m\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the unique \(a/b\) satisfying \(|a|\le A\), \(0<b\le B\), \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), and \(a\equiv rb\pmod m\), or reports failure.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical bounded rational reconstruction uniqueness criterion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is modular rational reconstruction from a residue, whereas the immutable path places the leaf under Safe Rational Recovery beside floating-point artifacts and safety validation. The selected algorithm addresses a materially different reconstruction setting.

children.title: Safety Validation
children.top_down_role: Independent validation of reconstructed certificate objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Safety Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validation criterion for a rationally reconstructed certificate artifact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the original floating-point artifact be \(z\), let rational reconstruction return \(\widehat z\in\mathbb Q^k\), and let \(V\) be the exact certificate checker. The reconstruction is safety-validated only if \(V(\widehat z)=\mathrm{accept}\) after every coefficient, bound, inference premise, and conclusion referenced by \(\widehat z\) has been evaluated using exact rational arithmetic. Acceptance certifies the encoded conclusion, not the numerical closeness of \(z\) and \(\widehat z\). If parsing, reconstruction, or any exact check is ambiguous or fails, the validator returns \(\mathrm{reject}\) or \(\mathrm{unknown}\), never acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reconstructed rational artifact is safe only when an exact checker validates every referenced inference; numerical proximity to the floating-point artifact is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat z\) is syntactically admissible for the certificate format.
\(V\) performs all semantic checks in exact rational arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(\widehat z)=\mathrm{accept}\) certifies the conclusion encoded by \(\widehat z\).

notation.meaning: Original floating-point artifact and its rational reconstruction.

review_flags: Exact certificate-interface semantics require a dedicated proof-logging source.
No supplied locator supports fail-closed rational-recovery validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fail-closed exact-validation criterion fits the leaf, and certificate is an acceptable role for the validation artifact, but no cited format specification or checker reference supports the claimed acceptance, rejection, and unknown semantics.

children.title: Recoverable Floating-Point Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Numerical outputs suitable for conversion into checkable rational objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Recoverable Floating-Point Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Artifacts admitting unique bounded-denominator rational reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer denominator bound \(Q\ge 1\). A scalar floating-point artifact \(y\in\mathbb R\) is \(Q\)-recoverable if there exists a unique reduced fraction \(p/q\) with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(1\le q\le Q\), and \(\lvert y-p/q\rvert<1/(2qQ)\). A vector artifact is \(Q\)-recoverable when every component is recoverable and the reconstructed vector satisfies all exact syntactic side conditions of its intended certificate record. The definition concerns recoverability only; semantic validity still requires exact certificate checking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An artifact is recoverable when each value uniquely identifies a bounded-denominator rational and the resulting record satisfies its exact format constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\).
Candidate fractions are represented in lowest terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstruction identifies at most one fraction \(p/q\) satisfying the stated bound.
review_flags: A source for the precise rational-reconstruction radius is required.
Certificate-specific syntactic recovery conditions depend on the chosen format.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and its candidate-dependent radius yields uniqueness, but the precise reconstruction criterion and certificate-format side conditions lack a source.

children.title: Reconstruction Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where numerical evidence cannot support safe rational recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Reconstruction Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambiguity, nonexistence, and validation-failure boundaries for bounded-denominator reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(Q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 2}\) and an acceptance radius \(\varepsilon\ge 0\). Safe reconstruction of \(y\in\mathbb R\) must fail when no reduced fraction \(p/q\) with \(p\in\mathbb Z\) and \(1\le q\le Q\) satisfies \(\lvert y-p/q\rvert\le\varepsilon\), or when more than one such fraction satisfies it. Distinct reduced fractions with denominators at most \(Q\) are separated by at least \(1/(Q(Q-1))\), and this bound is attained. Consequently, \(2\varepsilon<1/(Q(Q-1))\) guarantees at most one admissible fraction uniformly, whereas \(2\varepsilon\ge 1/(Q(Q-1))\) permits ambiguity for some observation. Reconstruction must also fail if the recovered record violates the certificate format or exact validation rejects it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery fails when no bounded-denominator rational fits, more than one fits, the tolerance reaches half the minimum Farey separation, or the reconstructed record fails format or exact validation checks.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 2}\).
\(y\in\mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon\ge 0\).
Only reduced fractions with denominators at most \(Q\) are admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform uniqueness is guaranteed by \(2\varepsilon<1/(Q(Q-1))\), while ambiguity is possible when \(2\varepsilon\ge 1/(Q(Q-1))\).
review_flags: A rational-reconstruction or Farey-sequence source is required.
Certificate-format failure behavior is format dependent.

children.title: Proof-Logging Feature Coverage
children.top_down_role: Supported and unsupported solver mechanisms within certificate formats.

knowledge_statements.title: Proof-Logging Feature Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage criterion for solver mechanisms represented by a certificate format.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a class of solver mechanisms, \(F\) a certificate format, and \(V_F\) its checker. A mechanism \(M\in\mathcal M\) is covered by \(F\) if every accepted solver use of \(M\) that contributes to the claimed result can be translated into a finite sequence of \(F\)-records whose premises are previously validated records or original constraints, and whose conclusions are validated by \(V_F\). It is unsupported if some required semantic effect of \(M\) has no such record sequence. An instance log is complete only if every result-contributing mechanism used on that run is covered and logged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A format covers a solver mechanism exactly when every result-relevant use can be translated into checker-validated records with established premises.
assumptions_latex: \(V_F\) has specified exact semantics for every record type in \(F\).

children.title: Cut Count Complexity
children.top_down_role: Number of inequalities appearing in cutting-plane derivations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Count Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of derived inequalities in a cutting-plane proof.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite cutting-plane derivation \(\pi=(I_1,\ldots,I_m)\) from an initial system \(Ax\le b\), its cut-count complexity is \(C(\pi)=m\), where each \(I_j\) is one newly derived inequality and repeated derivations are counted separately. For a target inequality \(I\), define \(C_{Ax\le b}(I)=\min\{C(\pi):\pi\text{ derives }I\}\), with value \(+\infty\) if no admissible derivation exists. For an infeasibility proof, the target may be any explicit contradiction, such as \(0\le-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut-count complexity is the minimum number of derived inequalities needed to obtain a target inequality or explicit contradiction.
assumptions_latex: A fixed cutting-plane inference system determines which derivations are admissible.
The initial inequalities are not counted as derived cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{Ax\le b}(I)\) measures proof size by cut count alone.

notation.meaning: Number of derived inequalities in the derivation.

review_flags: The supplied section supports cutting-plane derivations; exact proof-complexity terminology should be checked.

children.title: Derivation Length Complexity
children.top_down_role: Sequential extent of cutting-plane derivations.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivation Length Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total binary encoding length of a cutting-plane derivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a self-delimiting binary encoding \(\operatorname{enc}\) for rational inequalities and their inference annotations. For a cutting-plane derivation \(\pi=(I_1,\ldots,I_m)\), its derivation-length complexity is \(L(\pi)=\sum_{j=1}^m\lvert\operatorname{enc}(I_j,\rho_j)\rvert\), where \(\rho_j\) records the rule, premises, and numerical multipliers used to derive \(I_j\). The minimum length for deriving target \(I\) from \(Ax\le b\) is \(L_{Ax\le b}(I)=\min_\pi L(\pi)\). Thus coefficient encodings and inference data contribute even when the number of cuts is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Derivation length is the total bit length of all derived inequalities and their inference annotations, minimized over proofs of the target.
assumptions_latex: All rational data use a fixed canonical binary encoding.
Each inference annotation identifies its rule and premises.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{Ax\le b}(I)\) measures the complete encoded size of a derivation of \(I\).

notation.meaning: Total encoded bit length of the derivation.
Inference annotation for the j-th derived inequality.

children.title: Count-Length Tradeoffs

knowledge_statements.title: Count-Length Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relations between cut count and encoded derivation length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under any encoding in which every derived inequality and annotation occupies at least one bit, every derivation \(\pi\) satisfies \(C(\pi)\le L(\pi)\). If each record has length at most \(B\), then \(L(\pi)\le B C(\pi)\). Consequently, polynomial cut count implies polynomial derivation length only when the maximum record length is also polynomially bounded. Conversely, polynomial derivation length always implies polynomial cut count under the stated encoding. No bound on cut count alone controls coefficient growth or total proof length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bit length always bounds cut count, but a small cut count yields a short proof only when every cut record is also short.
assumptions_latex: Every derived-cut record has positive integral encoding length.
\(B\) bounds the bit length of every record in \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(\pi)\le L(\pi)\le B C(\pi)\).

notation.meaning: Maximum encoded length of one derivation record.

children.title: Coefficient Representation Complexity

children.title: Coefficient Magnitude Complexity
children.top_down_role: Magnitude growth among coefficients in intermediate inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Magnitude Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Largest absolute coefficient in the canonical primitive integer representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonzero rational inequality \(a^\top x\le\beta\), let \((\bar a,\bar\beta)\in\mathbb Z^{n+1}\) be its canonical primitive integer representative: \((\bar a,\bar\beta)=\lambda(a,\beta)\) for some \(\lambda>0\), the entries of \((\bar a,\bar\beta)\) have greatest common divisor \(1\), and a fixed sign convention is used. Define \(M(a,\beta)=\max\{1,\lvert\bar\beta\rvert,\lvert\bar a_1\rvert,\ldots,\lvert\bar a_n\rvert\}\). For a nonempty finite derivation \(\pi\), define \(M(\pi)=\max_{I\in\pi}M(I)\). The unsigned magnitude of every coefficient can then be stored using at most \(\lceil\log_2(M(\pi)+1)\rceil\) bits, and a coefficient attaining magnitude \(M(\pi)\) requires that many unsigned magnitude bits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient-magnitude complexity is the largest absolute coefficient in the canonical primitive integer representation of an inequality or derivation; its binary magnitude uses the ceiling of log base two of one plus that value.
assumptions_latex: \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb Q^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\).
Positive scaling preserves the inequality orientation.
Primitive normalization uses a fixed sign convention.
\(\pi\) is a nonempty finite derivation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum unsigned coefficient-magnitude length is \(\lceil\log_2(M(\pi)+1)\rceil\) bits.

notation.meaning: Canonical primitive integer representative of the rational inequality.
Maximum absolute coefficient of the normalized inequality, lower-bounded by one.

children.title: Inequality Sparsity
children.top_down_role: Support size of inequalities appearing in derivations.

knowledge_statements.title: Inequality Sparsity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support size of inequalities occurring in a derivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inequality \(a^\top x\le\beta\) in \(n\) variables, its support is \(\operatorname{supp}(a)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:a_i\ne0\}\), and its sparsity is \(s(a)=\lvert\operatorname{supp}(a)\rvert\). For a cutting-plane derivation \(\pi\), define maximum inequality sparsity by \(s(\pi)=\max_{I\in\pi}s(I)\). The corresponding density is \(s(a)/n\). The right-hand side and inference annotations are excluded from support size unless a separate augmented-row convention is explicitly adopted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inequality sparsity counts nonzero variable coefficients; derivation sparsity is the maximum such count among its derived inequalities.
assumptions_latex: All inequalities use the same ordered set of \(n\) variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le s(a)\le n\) and \(0\le s(\pi)\le n\).

notation.meaning: Maximum support size in a derivation.

children.title: Encoding-Length Consequences
children.top_down_role: Representation costs induced by coefficient magnitude and support size.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Length Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-size bound from cut count, sparsity, and coefficient magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a derivation \(\pi\) with \(C\) derived inequalities, at most \(s\) nonzero variable coefficients per inequality, and primitive integer coefficients of magnitude at most \(M\). Under a sparse binary encoding that stores each index and signed coefficient explicitly, the inequality data occupy \(O\!\left(C\bigl(s(\log n+\log(M+1))+\log(M+1)\bigr)\right)\) bits. Premise indices and rule annotations must be added separately. Hence polynomial bounds on \(C\), \(s\), \(\log(M+1)\), and annotation length yield polynomial total derivation length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse proof encoding is polynomial when cut count, support size, coefficient bit size, and inference annotations are all polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: Variables are indexed in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Each nonzero coefficient is stored as an index and signed binary integer.
Every inequality is in primitive integer form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality-data length is \(O\!\left(C\bigl(s(\log n+\log(M+1))+\log(M+1)\bigr)\right)\).

children.title: Density Growth Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where increasingly dense inequalities become impractical.

knowledge_statements.title: Density Growth Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of sparse-encoding advantages as derived cuts become dense.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi_n\) be derivations over \(n\) variables. If some derived inequality has support size \(s_n=\Theta(n)\), then every explicit sparse encoding of that inequality requires \(\Omega(n)\) coefficient-index entries, even when all coefficient magnitudes are bounded. Thus a sparsity-based sublinear row-size guarantee fails once density \(s_n/n\) is bounded away from zero. More generally, combining inequalities may produce support equal to the union of their supports unless exact cancellation occurs, so inference rules do not preserve sparsity without an additional structural hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once a derived cut contains a constant fraction of all variables, explicit sparse storage costs linear space and sparsity guarantees disappear.
assumptions_latex: Each nonzero coefficient is explicitly represented.
The variable dimension \(n\) tends to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_n=\Theta(n)\) implies an explicit row-encoding lower bound of \(\Omega(n)\) entries.

notation.meaning: Support size of a derived inequality in dimension n.

children.title: Rank-Depth Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connection from algorithmic proof length to closure and rank theory.

children.title: Cutting-Plane Rank
children.top_down_role: Closure-based rank measures relevant to cutting-plane derivations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum number of closure rounds needed to obtain an inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a cutting-plane closure operator \(\mathcal C\) on rational polyhedra and define \(P^{(0)}=P\) and \(P^{(r+1)}=\mathcal C(P^{(r)})\). For an inequality \(a^\top x\le\beta\) valid for the intended integer set, its \(\mathcal C\)-rank relative to \(P\) is the least \(r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) such that the inequality is valid for \(P^{(r)}\); its rank is \(+\infty\) if no such \(r\) exists. The rank of a target polyhedron is the least round at which all inequalities defining that target are valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cutting-plane rank is the fewest successive closure rounds required before a target inequality, or every inequality of a target polyhedron, becomes valid.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a rational polyhedron.
\(\mathcal C(P)\subseteq P\) is the fixed cutting-plane closure under study.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal C,P}(a,\beta)=\min\{r:a^\top x\le\beta\text{ is valid for }P^{(r)}\}\).

notation.meaning: Rank relative to the closure and initial relaxation.

review_flags: The supplied locator discusses cutting planes but may not contain the closure-rank definition.
Closure family must remain explicit because ranks differ across cutting-plane systems.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inequality-rank definition is standard and correctly keeps the closure family explicit, but the cited introductory cutting-plane section is not a specific locator for closure rank. Moreover, rank of a target polyhedron via 'all inequalities defining that target' depends on the chosen defining system unless formulated as the first round whose closure is contained in the target.

children.title: Derivation Depth
children.top_down_role: Layered depth of dependencies within cut derivations.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a rational relaxation of \(F=P\cap(\mathbb{Z}^p\times\mathbb{R}^{n-p})\).
For every relaxation \(Q\supseteq F\), \(\mathcal C(Q)\) is the fixed collection of inequalities generated by the specified cutting-plane rule and valid for \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathcal C}(a,b;P)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:a^\top x\le b\text{ is valid for }P_t\}\), with value \(+\infty\) when the set is empty.

notation.meaning: Relaxation after t canonical parallel closure rounds
Derivation depth of the target inequality

review_flags: exact proof-system convention requires a dedicated source
standard_field_rationale: round depth is the least number of canonical parallel cut-generation rounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical round depth relative to a fixed cutting rule and initial relaxation; alternative proof-sequence conventions require separate definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(P_0=P\) and, for each \(t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), define \(P_{t+1}=P_t\cap\bigcap\{x:a^\top x\le b\mid (a,b)\in\mathcal C(P_t)\}\). The \(\mathcal C\)-derivation depth of an inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) valid for \(F\) is the least \(t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for which it is valid for \(P_t\). The refutation depth is the least \(t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for which \(P_t=\varnothing\). If the relevant set of rounds is empty, the depth is \(+\infty\). All cuts used to form \(P_{t+1}\) are generated from \(P_t\), so cuts in the same round cannot depend on one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Derivation depth is the number of canonical parallel applications of a fixed cutting rule needed to establish a target inequality or obtain an empty relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivation Depth

children.title: Rank-Depth Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between closure rank and derivation depth.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and the cutting rule \(\mathcal C\) are fixed.
Rank and depth use the same parallel-round derivability convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_{\mathcal C}(a,b;P)=d_{\mathcal C}(a,b;P)\), and \(r_{\mathcal C}(P)=d_{\mathcal C}(P)\) for refutations.
review_flags: correspondence depends on matching rank and derivation conventions
exact proof-system convention requires a dedicated source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality under matched parallel-round definitions, not across different proof systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the \(\mathcal C\)-rank of a valid inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) as the least integer \(t\ge 0\) such that the inequality is valid after \(t\) iterated applications of the closure induced by \(\mathcal C\). Define derivation depth using parallel levels, where every cut at level \(t+1\) is derivable solely from inequalities available through level \(t\). Under these matched conventions, an inequality has rank at most \(t\) exactly when it admits a derivation of depth at most \(t\). The same equivalence holds for refutations when the target conclusion is \(P_t=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When rank iterations and proof levels use identical rules, cutting-plane rank equals minimum parallel derivation depth.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Depth Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The correspondence is correct only by matching the closure-rank and parallel-level conventions exactly. No citation is supplied for those conventions or for the refutation extension, so the mathematical version remains source-dependent.

children.title: Rank-Depth Interface Limitations
children.top_down_role: Cases where rank does not adequately predict derivation complexity.

assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a derivation in a cutting system that permits arbitrarily many mutually independent cuts at one parallel level.
\(r(D)\) is the number of dependency levels in \(D\), and \(S(D)\) counts the derived inequalities or their total encoded length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For arbitrary derivations, \(r(D)\) alone does not impose an upper bound on \(S(D)\); this observation does not by itself prove a separation between minimum rank and minimum proof size for a fixed conclusion.

notation.meaning: Parallel dependency depth of derivation D
Number or encoded size of inequalities in derivation D

review_flags: minimum-proof-size separations require a dedicated source
exact proof-system and size conventions require a dedicated source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank controls dependency rounds of a derivation, not its width, encoded size, coefficient complexity, or the global validity of branch-local cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Rank-depth correspondence does not identify the size of an arbitrary derivation. If \(m\) mutually independent inequalities are all derived from the initial relaxation, a derivation containing them has \(r(D)=1\) and may have \(S(D)\ge m\), for arbitrarily large \(m\). Conversely, a sequential chain in which each inequality depends on its predecessor can have depth equal to its number of derivation steps. These observations concern particular derivations; a lower bound on the minimum proof size for a fixed conclusion requires a separate proof-system-specific result. Moreover, an inequality valid only at a branch node has no global rank unless a specified lifting or disjunctive inference produces a globally valid inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependency depth does not determine the size of a particular derivation, and branch-local cuts do not automatically possess global rank; minimum-size separations require additional results.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Depth Interface Limitations

children.title: Cutting-over-Branching Advantage Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes admitting substantially shorter cutting-plane derivations.

assumptions_latex: \((I_k)_{k\ge1}\) is an instance family with encoding length \(L_k\).
Cutting and branching proof systems and their size measures are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cut}(I_k)=L_k^{O(1)}\) and \(\operatorname{Br}(I_k)=2^{\Omega(L_k^\alpha)}\) for some \(\alpha>0\).
review_flags: candidate formalization of an advantage regime
concrete separating families and proof systems require sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic proof-size separation for explicitly fixed cutting and branching systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((I_k)_{k\ge1}\) lies in a cutting-over-branching advantage regime when there is a constant \(c\ge1\) such that \(\operatorname{Cut}(I_k)\le L_k^c\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), while there exist constants \(\alpha,c'>0\) such that \(\operatorname{Br}(I_k)\ge 2^{c'L_k^\alpha}\) for infinitely many \(k\). Both minima must certify the same conclusion, such as infeasibility or a common objective bound, and preprocessing, coefficient encoding, admissible cuts, branching disjunctions, and leaf certificates must be held fixed across the comparison.

children.title: Branching-over-Cutting Advantage Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes in which subdivision outperforms restricted cutting systems.

assumptions_latex: \((I_k)_{k\ge1}\) is an instance family with encoding length \(L_k\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Br}(I_k)=L_k^{O(1)}\) and \(\operatorname{Cut}(I_k)=2^{\Omega(L_k^\alpha)}\) for some \(\alpha>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((I_k)_{k\ge1}\) lies in a branching-over-cutting advantage regime when some constant \(c\ge1\) satisfies \(\operatorname{Br}(I_k)\le L_k^c\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), but constants \(\alpha,c'>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{Cut}(I_k)\ge 2^{c'L_k^\alpha}\) for infinitely many \(k\). Allowing an unrestricted cut family can invalidate the separation by encoding the branching disjunction directly.

children.title: Branching-Cutting Synthesis
children.top_down_role: Regimes where combining branching and cutting is stronger than either alone.

children.title: Branching-Supported Cut Strength
children.top_down_role: Cutting advantages enabled by subdivision of the feasible region.

assumptions_latex: A branch node has relaxation \(P_v\) and integer-feasible set \(F_v\).
\(\mathcal C(P_v)\) denotes cuts derivable under the fixed local rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal C}(a^\top x\le b;P_v)<\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal C}(a^\top x\le b;P)\), allowing \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Cutting-plane rank relative to a relaxation

review_flags: specific cut families exhibiting strict improvement require sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local branches may lower the rank of inequalities relevant to that subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Branching supports the strength of a cut \(a^\top x\le b\), valid for \(F_v\), when restricting the parent relaxation \(P\) to a branch node \(P_v\) strictly lowers the cut's derivation rank under the same rule \(\mathcal C\). Formally, the local rank is smaller than the parent rank, with an underivable parent inequality assigned rank \(+\infty\). This is a local statement: unless \(a^\top x\le b\) is valid for the entire integer-feasible set or is combined across all children by a valid disjunctive inference, the locally strengthened inequality cannot be installed globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching supports cut strength when a branch restriction lowers the derivation rank of a locally valid inequality under the same cutting rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Supported Cut Strength

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches the local notion of branching-supported cut strength, including the local-versus-global validity warning. Its strict rank comparison and the convention assigning parent rank \(+\infty\) require a source tied to a specified cutting system.

children.title: Cutting-Supported Tree Reduction
children.top_down_role: Search-tree reductions enabled by relaxation strengthening.

assumptions_latex: \(T(P)\) is a branching tree proving a fixed conclusion from relaxation \(P\).
\(P'\subseteq P\) is obtained by adding inequalities valid for the integer-feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(P')\le B(P)\), with strict reduction when \(B(P')<B(P)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of nodes in an admissible branching proof

review_flags: strict-reduction criteria depend on the branching and leaf-certificate models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic tree-size comparison under globally valid relaxation strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B(P)\) be the minimum number of nodes in a branching tree that certifies a fixed conclusion from \(P\), using fixed branching disjunctions and a leaf-certification rule monotone under set inclusion. If globally valid cuts replace \(P\) by \(P'\subseteq P\), every leaf region feasible for \(P'\) is contained in the corresponding region for \(P\). Hence any tree valid for \(P\) remains valid for \(P'\), and \(B(P')\le B(P)\). Cutting-supported tree reduction occurs when the inequality is strict; mere relaxation strengthening guarantees nonincrease, not strict improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Globally valid cuts cannot enlarge the smallest tree under monotone leaf certification, and support tree reduction precisely when the inequality is strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Supported Tree Reduction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonicity property is mathematically coherent under the explicitly assumed inclusion-monotone leaf rule, and the content kind fits the container. No source supports this proof model or the strict-reduction interpretation.

children.title: Complementary Advantage Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes where integrated branching and cutting outperform either component.

assumptions_latex: \((I_k)\) is an instance family and \(L_k\) is its encoding length.
Pure cutting, pure branching, and combined proof systems use fixed inference and size conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(I_k)=L_k^{O(1)}\), while \(C(I_k),B(I_k)=2^{\Omega(L_k^\alpha)}\) for some \(\alpha>0\).
review_flags: candidate definition of strong complementary advantage
concrete families establishing simultaneous separation require sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong synergy means the combined system is asymptotically smaller than either pure subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((I_k)\) exhibits a strong complementary advantage when a combined branching-cutting proof has polynomial size, but every proof in either pure subsystem has exponential size. Concretely, for some constants \(c,c',\alpha>0\), one has \(H(I_k)\le L_k^c\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), while \(C(I_k)\ge2^{c'L_k^\alpha}\) and \(B(I_k)\ge2^{c'L_k^\alpha}\) for infinitely many \(k\). All three systems must certify the same conclusion and charge consistently for cuts, branch nodes, coefficients, and leaf certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong complementary advantage occurs when integrated proofs are polynomial although both pure cutting and pure branching proofs are exponential.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits a strong complementary-advantage regime, but simultaneous exponential lower bounds for both pure systems and a polynomial upper bound for the hybrid system are highly proof-system-specific. No supporting family or citation is provided.

children.title: Synergy Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes where integration offers little comparative benefit.

assumptions_latex: \(C(I)\), \(B(I)\), and \(H(I)\) are minimum proof sizes under fixed compatible conventions.
The combined system contains the pure cutting and pure branching systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(I_k)\ge q(\min\{C(I_k),B(I_k)\})\) throughout the family.
review_flags: candidate quantitative boundary for synergy failure
appropriate comparison function depends on the proof model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absence of asymptotic gain beyond the better pure proof system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a nondecreasing comparison function \(q:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}_+\). A family \((I_k)\) is a synergy-failure regime at scale \(q\) when every combined proof satisfies \(H(I_k)\ge q(\min\{C(I_k),B(I_k)\})\). Since the combined system contains both pure systems, one also has \(H(I_k)\le\min\{C(I_k),B(I_k)\}\). Thus choosing \(q(s)=s^{1/c}\) for a constant \(c\ge1\) excludes any superpolynomial improvement of the integrated system over the better pure system. The claim is relative to identical conclusions and compatible accounting conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synergy fails at a chosen scale when combined proofs cannot asymptotically improve beyond that scale over the better pure proof.
knowledge_statements.title: Synergy Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scale-dependent condition is internally compatible with containment of the pure systems, but it is a proposed quantitative definition rather than a sourced standard boundary. The appropriate comparison function and accounting conventions depend on the proof model.

children.title: Dimension-Sensitive Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparative behavior when dimension is treated as a fixed parameter.

assumptions_latex: Instances are rational mixed-integer systems in dimension \(d\).
Cutting, branching, and encoding conventions are fixed for every \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_d(L)=\sup\{C(I)/B(I):\dim(I)=d,\ \operatorname{len}(I)\le L\}\) is the dimension-sensitive comparison profile.

notation.meaning: Worst-case size ratio at dimension d and length L

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed dimension is separated from binary input length and proof-system parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed dimension \(d\) and input-length bound \(L\), define the cutting-to-branching profile by \(R_d(L)=\sup\{C(I)/B(I):\dim(I)=d,\operatorname{len}(I)\le L,B(I)>0\}\). The reciprocal profile is defined analogously. A comparison is dimension-sensitive only if its constants and exponents may depend on \(d\), while their dependence on \(L\) is stated explicitly. Fixing \(d\) alone does not establish polynomial proof size: the admissible cuts, branching disjunctions, coefficient lengths, separation cost, and leaf certificates remain part of the complexity model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension-sensitive profile compares minimum proof sizes at fixed dimension while retaining binary input length and proof-system conventions as explicit parameters.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Sensitive Comparison

children.title: Relaxation Progress Failure Family
children.top_down_role: Failures in which valid cuts do not yield useful progress or make the active relaxation unmanageable.

children.title: Separation Stagnation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Weak or diminishing progress over successive separation rounds.

children.title: Separation Stall
children.top_down_role: Failure to obtain useful relaxation strengthening from separation.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is the current relaxation of a minimization problem, \(\bar x\in P\) is a current optimizer, and \(z(Q)\) denotes the relaxation bound over a set \(Q\).
\(\mathcal C\) is a specified family of valid inequalities, \(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal C}(P)\) is its closure, and \(\mathcal S\) is the implemented separation procedure.
\(P^{\mathcal S}\subseteq P\) is the relaxation obtained by adding all cuts returned by \(\mathcal S\) in the current separation call.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A separation stall occurs if either \(\mathcal S(\bar x)=\mathrm{NONE}\) while \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal C}(P)\), or \(z(P^{\mathcal S})=z(P)<z(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal C}(P))\).

notation.meaning: Closure under all cuts in the specified family
Relaxation produced by cuts returned in the current separation call
Relaxation bound for a minimization problem

review_flags: candidate distinction between point-separation stall, bound-progress stall, and closure exhaustion
solver-specific separation behavior requires a dedicated source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the implemented separator to realize an exclusion or bound improvement available from the full specified cut closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point-separation stall occurs at \(\bar x\) when \(\mathcal S(\bar x)=\mathrm{NONE}\) although \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal C}(P)\). A bound-progress stall occurs when the returned cuts produce \(P^{\mathcal S}\) with \(z(P^{\mathcal S})=z(P)\), although \(z(P)<z(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal C}(P))\). Either event records failure of the implemented procedure to realize progress available from the full cut family. If \(\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal C}(P)\) and \(z(P)=z(\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal C}(P))\), the event is closure exhaustion rather than separation stall.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation stalls when the implemented procedure misses either a point exclusion or a bound improvement that remains available from the full specified cut closure.
knowledge_statements.title: Separation Stall

children.title: Tailing-Off Regimes
children.top_down_role: Successive separation rounds with diminishing bound improvement.

assumptions_latex: \((P_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a nested sequence of minimization relaxations with \(P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t\).
For every \(t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), \(z_t=z(P_t)\) is finite and satisfies \(z_t<z_{t+1}\).
The sequence \((z_t)_{t\ge0}\) converges to a finite limit \(z_\infty\) that is not attained at any finite \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_t<z_\infty\) for every \(t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and \(z_{t+1}-z_t\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: Relaxation objective bound at round t

review_flags: candidate quantitative condition for tailing off
threshold-based and relative-gap variants require separate sourcing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly improving bounds converge without finite attainment while their absolute marginal improvements vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cutting sequence is in this tailing-off regime when \(P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t\), the finite bounds satisfy \(z_t<z_{t+1}<z_\infty\) for every \(t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and \(z_t\to z_\infty\). These conditions imply \(z_{t+1}-z_t\to0\). The additional relative-gap condition \((z_{t+1}-z_t)/(z_\infty-z_t)\to0\) defines a stronger, scale-free tailing-off regime and is not implied by vanishing absolute gains alone. Finite attainment and a uniformly positive fraction of the remaining gap per round lie outside that stronger regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tailing off means that relaxation bounds improve strictly toward an unattained finite limit while the absolute gain per round vanishes; requiring the gain to be a vanishing fraction of the remaining gap is a stronger condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Tailing-Off Regimes

children.title: Progress Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Signals used to distinguish productive separation from stagnation.

knowledge_statements.title: Progress Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational diagnostics for successive cut-generation rounds in a minimization branch-and-cut node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let round \(k\) have valid lower bound \(z_k\), separation time \(s_k>0\), generated-cut set \(G_k\), retained set \(R_k\subseteq G_k\), and maximum generated-cut violation \(v_k\ge 0\). Define the progress diagnostic vector by \[D_k=\left(z_k-z_{k-1},\;\frac{z_k-z_{k-1}}{s_k},\;\frac{|R_k|}{\max\{1,|G_k|\}},\;v_k\right).\] The components respectively measure bound improvement, improvement per separation-time unit, cut-retention yield, and residual separation strength. Over a window \(W_k=\{k-w+1,\ldots,k\}\), progress is summarized by the componentwise median of \(\{D_j:j\in W_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Track bound gain, gain per separation time, retention yield, and maximum violation; window medians distinguish productive cutting from tailing off or separation stall.
assumptions_latex: \(z_k\ge z_{k-1}\) for valid minimization lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_k\) and its window median provide explicitly computable progress diagnostics.

notation.meaning: Relaxation lower bound after round k.

children.title: Stagnation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions supporting termination or suspension of unproductive separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Stagnation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Windowed boundary between productive separation and negligible relaxation progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization relaxation, fix a window length \(w\ge 1\), bound tolerance \(\varepsilon_z\ge 0\), and violation tolerance \(\varepsilon_v\ge 0\). With lower bounds \(z_j\) and maximum violations \(v_j\), round \(k\) lies in the stagnation region precisely when \[z_k-z_{k-w}\le \varepsilon_z\quad\text{and}\quad \max_{k-w<j\le k}v_j\le \varepsilon_v.\] Its boundary is the union of the equality surfaces obtained by replacing either inequality with equality while retaining the other. Crossing outside this region requires a bound gain exceeding \(\varepsilon_z\) or a detected violation exceeding \(\varepsilon_v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation is stagnant when both windowed bound improvement and all detected violations remain below prescribed tolerances; equality identifies the stagnation boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(z_j\) are valid nondecreasing lower bounds.
\(k\ge w\), \(\varepsilon_z,\varepsilon_v\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_k-z_{k-w}\le\varepsilon_z\) and \(\max_{k-w<j\le k}v_j\le\varepsilon_v\) characterize the chosen stagnation region.

children.title: Hard-Separation Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Cut-generation cost that overwhelms expected bounding benefit.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Separation Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-benefit and budgeted boundaries for exact or expensive cut separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At search state \(k\), let \(C_k^{\mathrm{sep}}\ge 0\) be the computational cost of running a separator and let \(B_k\ge 0\) be the expected downstream computation saved by the resulting cuts, measured in the same cost units and conditional on current information. The cost-benefit hard-separation boundary is \[C_k^{\mathrm{sep}}=B_k,\] with a bottleneck diagnosed when \(C_k^{\mathrm{sep}}\ge B_k\). Separately, given observed bound improvement \(\Delta z_k\ge 0\) and a budget \(\rho>0\) per bound unit, a budgeted diagnostic declares a bottleneck when \[\Delta z_k=0\quad\text{or}\quad \frac{C_k^{\mathrm{sep}}}{\Delta z_k}\ge\rho.\] These diagnostics coincide only under an additional model relating \(B_k\) to \(\Delta z_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost-benefit bottleneck occurs when separation cost meets or exceeds its expected downstream saving. A separate budgeted diagnostic flags zero bound improvement or excessive cost per bound-improvement unit; the two tests are not generally equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(C_k^{\mathrm{sep}}\) and \(B_k\) use identical computational cost units.
\(C_k^{\mathrm{sep}},B_k,\Delta z_k\ge0\) and \(\rho>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_k^{\mathrm{sep}}\ge B_k\) defines the cost-benefit bottleneck, while the ratio test defines a distinct budgeted bottleneck.

notation.meaning: Observed bound improvement attributable to separation.
Maximum acceptable separation cost per bound-improvement unit.

children.title: Relaxation Overload Boundary
children.top_down_role: Relaxation growth whose computational cost exceeds its strengthening benefit.

children.title: Active-Cut Overload
children.top_down_role: Excessive active-cut populations within node relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Cut Overload
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational overload condition based on nearly binding retained cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the relaxation at round \(k\) with retained cuts \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), \(i\in R_k\), and optimal solution \(x_k\). For activity tolerance \(\varepsilon_a\ge0\), define \[A_k=\left\{i\in R_k:0\le b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k\le\varepsilon_a\max\{1,|b_i|\}\right\}.\] Given an absolute limit \(M_a\) and relative limit \(\alpha_a\in(0,1]\), active-cut overload occurs when \[|A_k|>M_a\quad\text{or}\quad |A_k|/\max\{1,n\}>\alpha_a,\] where \(n\) is the number of relaxation variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active-cut overload occurs when the number of nearly binding retained cuts exceeds either an absolute cap or a variable-scaled cap.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k\) is feasible for every retained cut.
\(M_a\ge0\), \(\varepsilon_a\ge0\), and \(\alpha_a\in(0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|A_k|>M_a\) or \(|A_k|/\max\{1,n\}>\alpha_a\) is the overload predicate.

notation.meaning: Set of retained cuts active within tolerance.

children.title: Relaxation Size Growth
children.top_down_role: Expansion of relaxation dimensions caused by retained cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Size Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bookkeeping identities for rows and nonzeros under cut retention and deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the initial relaxation contain \(m_0\) rows and \(q_0\) nonzero coefficients. At round \(j\), let \(R_j\) be the cuts added and \(D_j\) the previously present cuts deleted; let \(s(c)\) denote the number of nonzero coefficients in cut \(c\). After \(k\) rounds, the relaxation dimensions satisfy \[m_k=m_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\bigl(|R_j|-|D_j|\bigr),\qquad q_k=q_0+\sum_{j=1}^k\left(\sum_{c\in R_j}s(c)-\sum_{c\in D_j}s(c)\right).\] Thus retaining cuts without deletion makes both quantities nondecreasing, and dense retained cuts can make \(q_k\) grow much faster than \(m_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rows grow by retained cuts minus deleted cuts; nonzeros grow by their support sizes, so dense retention can outpace row-count growth.
assumptions_latex: \(R_j\) and \(D_j\) count only actual row insertions and deletions.
Each cut has finite support size \(s(c)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed identities exactly determine relaxation row and nonzero growth.

notation.meaning: Row and nonzero counts after round k.
Cuts inserted and deleted in round j.

children.title: Solve-Time Degradation
children.top_down_role: Optimization cost increases attributable to enlarged relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Solve-Time Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Windowed condition detecting slower relaxation solves without compensating bound progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t_j>0\) be the relaxation solve time and \(z_j\) the valid minimization lower bound after cut round \(j\). Fix a baseline median \(t_{\mathrm{base}}>0\), window length \(w\), slowdown factor \(\gamma>1\), and minimum acceptable progress rate \(r_{\min}\ge0\). Solve-time degradation is diagnosed at round \(k\) when \[\operatorname{median}_{k-w<j\le k}t_j\ge\gamma t_{\mathrm{base}}\quad\text{and}\quad \frac{z_k-z_{k-w}}{\sum_{j=k-w+1}^{k}t_j}\le r_{\min}.\] The first inequality detects sustained slowdown; the second excludes slowdown compensated by sufficient bound improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degradation means median relaxation time exceeds its baseline factor while bound improvement per total solve time remains below an accepted rate.
assumptions_latex: \(k\ge w\ge1\) and \(t_j,t_{\mathrm{base}}>0\).
\(z_j\) are valid nondecreasing lower bounds.
\(\gamma>1\) and \(r_{\min}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjunction of the slowdown and low-progress-rate inequalities defines solve-time degradation.

notation.meaning: Relaxation solve time after round j.
Minimum acceptable bound gain per time unit.

children.title: Cut-Retention Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Boundaries where retaining additional cuts ceases to be beneficial.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Retention Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Score-threshold rule balancing cut efficacy against relaxation footprint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each valid candidate cut \(c\), compute normalized efficacy \(e(c)\ge0\), orthogonality score \(d(c)\in[0,1]\) relative to retained cuts, support density \(p(c)\in[0,1]\), and estimated numerical-risk score \(u(c)\in[0,1]\). Given nonnegative weights \(\lambda_e,\lambda_d,\lambda_p,\lambda_u\), define \[S(c)=\lambda_e e(c)+\lambda_d d(c)-\lambda_p p(c)-\lambda_u u(c).\] Retain \(c\) exactly when \(S(c)\ge\tau\), subject to a round cap \(M\): if more than \(M\) cuts qualify, retain the \(M\) largest-scoring cuts, breaking ties deterministically. Output the selected cut set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain valid cuts whose weighted efficacy and diversity outweigh density and numerical risk, subject to a deterministic per-round cap.
assumptions_latex: Every candidate cut is valid for its intended scope.
\(M\in\mathbb N\) and all score weights are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns at most \(M\) qualifying cuts with largest score \(S(c)\).

notation.meaning: Retention score of candidate cut c.

children.title: Cut Collection Quality Failures
children.top_down_role: Loss of efficiency and stability from poorly diversified cut collections.

children.title: Dense Cut Accumulation
children.top_down_role: Growth of cut collections dominated by broad variable support.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Cut Accumulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density-based condition for excessive nonzero growth in a retained cut pool.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For retained cuts \(R_k\) in \(n\) variables, let \(s(c)=|\{i:a_{ci}\ne0\}|\) be the support size of cut \(c\). Define average cut density and cumulative cut nonzeros by \[\bar d_k=\frac{1}{|R_k|}\sum_{c\in R_k}\frac{s(c)}{n},\qquad Q_k=\sum_{c\in R_k}s(c),\] with \(\bar d_k=0\) when \(R_k=\varnothing\). Given thresholds \(\delta\in(0,1]\) and \(Q_{\max}>0\), dense cut accumulation occurs when \[\bar d_k\ge\delta\quad\text{and}\quad Q_k>Q_{\max}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense cut accumulation occurs when retained cuts have high average support density and their total nonzero count exceeds a memory or factorization budget.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge1\) and every retained cut has finite support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar d_k\ge\delta\) and \(Q_k>Q_{\max}\) define dense cut accumulation.

notation.meaning: Number of variables occurring in cut c.

children.title: Redundant Cut Accumulation
children.top_down_role: Growth of cut collections containing overlapping strengthening information.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Cut Accumulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pool-level condition based on logical redundancy over the current relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_k\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the base relaxation and let \(R_k\) be retained inequalities. A cut \(c=(a_c,b_c)\in R_k\), representing \(a_c^{\mathsf T}x\le b_c\), is redundant relative to the remaining pool when \[P_k\cap\bigcap_{d\in R_k\setminus\{c\}}\{x:a_d^{\mathsf T}x\le b_d\}\subseteq\{x:a_c^{\mathsf T}x\le b_c\}.\] Let \(U_k\) be the set of such cuts. For a threshold \(\eta\in[0,1]\), redundant cut accumulation occurs when \(|U_k|/\max\{1,|R_k|\}\ge\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A retained cut is redundant if all other current constraints imply it; accumulation occurs when redundant cuts occupy a prescribed pool fraction.
assumptions_latex: \(P_k\) and every retained inequality are defined in the same space \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|U_k|/\max\{1,|R_k|\}\ge\eta\) is the redundant-accumulation predicate.

notation.meaning: Cuts implied by the base relaxation and remaining pool.

children.title: Cut-Diversity Loss
children.top_down_role: Concentration of retained cuts around similar relaxation features.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Diversity Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Angular diversity condition for normalized cut normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the nonzero normals of retained cuts be \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\), and normalize them as \(u_i=a_i/\|a_i\|_2\). Define angular diversity by \[D_k=1-\frac{2}{m(m-1)}\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}|u_i^{\mathsf T}u_j|\] for \(m\ge2\), and set \(D_k=1\) for \(m<2\). Then \(D_k\in[0,1]\). Given \(\delta_D\in[0,1]\), cut-diversity loss occurs when \(D_k\le\delta_D\); small values mean that many retained normals are parallel or antiparallel and therefore explore few distinct constraint directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut diversity is lost when the average absolute cosine similarity of normalized cut normals is so high that angular diversity falls below a threshold.
assumptions_latex: Every retained cut normal is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_k\le\delta_D\) defines angular cut-diversity loss.

notation.meaning: Normalized normal of retained cut i.

children.title: Numerical Stability Consequences
children.top_down_role: Stability degradation associated with dense or repetitive cut collections.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Stability Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning consequence of nearly dependent active cut rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a nonsingular basis matrix of an LP relaxation and suppose coefficient and right-hand-side perturbations satisfy \(\|B^{-1}\Delta B\|<1\). If \(Bx=b\) and \((B+\Delta B)(x+\Delta x)=b+\Delta b\), then \[\frac{\|\Delta x\|}{\|x\|}\le\frac{\kappa(B)}{1-\|B^{-1}\Delta B\|}\left(\frac{\|\Delta B\|}{\|B\|}+\frac{\|\Delta b\|}{\|b\|}\right).\] Consequently, adding dense or nearly dependent active cut rows that increase \(\kappa(B)=\|B\|\|B^{-1}\|\) enlarges the worst-case sensitivity bound, potentially degrading feasibility and reduced-cost tests performed with fixed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearly dependent active cuts can increase basis conditioning, amplifying coefficient and right-hand-side errors and weakening fixed-tolerance feasibility or reduced-cost decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular and \(b\ne0\), \(x\ne0\).
The matrix and vector norms are compatible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Larger \(\kappa(B)\) increases the displayed worst-case relative solution-error bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied for the exact perturbation inequality or for the asserted connection between accumulated cut rows, basis conditioning, and solver tests. These nontrivial claims require authoritative numerical linear algebra and LP-solver sources.

children.title: Invalid Global Cuts
children.top_down_role: Globally installed inequalities that exclude feasible integer solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Global Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Witness certificate that a globally installed inequality is not valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^{n-p}\) be the feasible set of the original mixed-integer problem. A globally installed inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) is invalid exactly when there exists \(x^\star\in X\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x^\star>b\). The point \(x^\star\), together with verifiable evidence that \(x^\star\in X\), is a certificate of global invalidity and identifies an original feasible mixed-integer solution excluded by the cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An original feasible mixed-integer point that violates a global cut certifies the cut’s invalidity and identifies a feasible solution removed by global installation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the original feasible mixed-integer set.
The inequality is installed globally rather than under a local node domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in X\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}x^\star>b\) certify that the global cut is invalid.

notation.meaning: Original feasible witness excluded by the cut.
